The Memory layer stores stable facts such as user preferences and environment configuration, using key-value or document form, auto-loaded at session start. The Skill layer stores standard operating procedures and best practices, using structured document form, actively loaded on demand by the agent. The Session Search layer uses FTS full-text indexing to store complete conversation history, supporting keyword search and LLM summarization. 1uxj9hp:278: Hermes introduces regex-based threat pattern recognition at the memory write layer—a pragmatic but limited security measure. It is pragmatic because it blocks the most common prompt injection patterns at extremely low computational cost, without requiring complex NLP models for semantic analysis. Its limitation is that regex cannot defend against semantic-level injection attacks (e.g., bypassing pattern matching through natural language descriptions). This suggests that for self-improving systems, prompt injection defense requires a multi-layer strategy—an input layer (regex/rule filtering), a reasoning layer (having the model judge content reasonableness before writing), and an audit layer (checking recorded content after the fact). Most current agent frameworks implement only the first layer, which is insufficient in highly adversarial scenarios.
1v95gpm:306: Hermes chooses to design dedicated tools for the skill mechanism (skill_list/skill_view/skill_manage) rather than using generic read/write tools to manipulate skill files—a design decision with deep engineering-philosophy considerations. Generic tools offer greater flexibility (one tool can handle all operations), but they increase the cognitive burden and error rate of model invocation; dedicated tools are less flexible but make the model's tool selection clearer and less error-prone. This reflects a core tension in agent system design: how to balance "tool specialization" against "tool unification." Hermes's answer is: for high-frequency, standardized operations (such as skill management), dedicated tools are superior to generic ones; for low-frequency, creative operations (such as arbitrary file editing), generic tools are more appropriate.
